claim: From 18 February 2027 each LMT battery, EV battery and industrial battery above 2 kWh placed on the market or put into service requires a battery passport with model and individual-battery data.

From 18 February 2027 covered batteries require a QR code leading to the passport; it must be visible, legible and indelible on the battery, or on packaging and accompanying documents where battery marking is impossible or unwarranted because of the battery's nature and size. The QR links to a placing-operator-assigned unique identifier and both must comply with the listed ISO/IEC 15459 family or equivalent.

claim: For reused, repurposed or remanufactured batteries, passport responsibility transfers to the new placing operator and a new passport must link to the original passport(s); new status markings are also required.
source_locator: excerpts/05-second-life-transfer.txt — Articles 13(9) and 77(7), PDF pages 24 and 84

claim: Operators placing reused, repurposed or remanufactured batteries must ensure examination, performance testing, packing and shipment follow adequate quality-control and safety instructions, and must ensure the batteries comply with the applicable rules.

The placing operator remains responsible for accurate, complete and current passport data even when another operator is authorised, and passport information must use open, interoperable, machine-readable formats without vendor lock-in.
Article 78 requires role-based access, continued availability, authentication, integrity, security/privacy and restricted processor reuse.

Since 18 August 2024 stationary BESS, LMT and EV batteries must contain current health/lifetime parameters in the BMS, with read-only access for purchasers and third parties acting on their behalf for specified purposes including valuation and repurposing.
The EU DPP Registry went live on 20 July 2026 with a testing environment; it stores identifiers/registration data while complete passport information is stored by the operator or provider.

claim: Article 77 divides passport information among public access, access for notified bodies/market-surveillance authorities/the Commission, and access for legitimate-interest persons for specified purposes.

Circularise markets ERP/PLM integration into a maintained passport record; this makes displacement of a separate external integration layer by a customer's source-system team a competitive inference to test.
The Regulation's open, interoperable, transferable and no-lock-in requirements may protect customer exit while increasing commoditisation pressure on a separate translation layer.
